chunks: Beware! You have broken the bonds of Islam, transgressed its limits, and destroyed its commands.

Beware! Surely Allah has commanded me to fight those who revolt, or who break the pledge, or create trouble on the earth. As regards pledge-breakers, I have fought them, as regards deviators from truth, I have waged holy war against them, and as regards those who have gone out of the faith, I have put them in (serious) disgrace.
As for Satan of the pit, he too has been dealt with by me through the loud cry with which the scream of his heart and shaking of his chest was also heard.
Only a small portion of the rebels has remained. If Allah allows me one more chance over them I will annihilate them except a few remnants that may remain scattered in the suburb of the cities.

key_terms.شَيْطَانُ الرَّدْهَةِ: Satan of the pit (referring to Amr ibn al-Kawth)

ai.seo_question: What are the three groups of rebels mentioned in Nahj al-Balagha and how did Imam Ali deal with them?
ai.summary: This passage from the Battle of Siffin sermon highlights Imam Ali’s (a) tripartite classification of rebel factions, a taxonomy later adopted by Shia scholars to distinguish between political dissenters and theological seceders. By identifying Amr ibn al-Kawth as 'Satan of the Pit,' the Imam emphasizes the spiritual corruption behind the military conflict, linking earthly battles to cosmic struggles. The concluding prophecy of total annihilation underscores the inevitability of divine justice against persistent injustice (Baghy).
